To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the signal intensities between different biofluids and between different analytes cannot be directly compared due to matrix effects and differences in ionization efficiencies, respectively, in non-quantified metabolomics.

(1) the signal intensity of a specific analyte in one matrix cannot be directly compared with the signal intensity of the same analyte in another matrix, (2) the signal intensity for any two analytes in the exact same matrix cannot be directly correlated to their relative abundance in that matrix.

the signal intensities in untargeted non-quantitative MS-based metabolomics cannot be directly compared between different biological matrices, and the signal intensities cannot be directly compared within the same matrix for different analytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of two well-recognized analytical issues in untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics: matrix effects and ion suppression.
the impact of matrix effect and ionization efficiency on untargeted metabolomic data analysis.
two important issues that can lead to misinterpretation of untargeted, metabolomics data: matrix effects and ion suppression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

signal intensities of any single analytes cannot be directly compared between any two matrices or to the signal intensity between any two analytes, even in the exact same matrix, without proper response corrections for matrix effects and ion suppression.

the signal intensities from any untargeted metabolomic experiment should not be compared between any two different biological matrices, nor between any two analytes in the experiment, unless the matrix effects and ion suppression effects are accounted for in the analysis.
the signal intensities in untargeted non-quantitative LC–MS metabolomics cannot be directly compared between any two different analytes in any two different biological matrices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the direct comparison of signal intensities in non-quantified metabolomics experiments, especially between matrices or between analytes in the absence of response correction, is not accurate.

signal intensities of any analyte cannot be compared to any other analyte without response correction in untargeted non-quantitative LC-MS metabolomics, and that the signal intensities between different matrices cannot be compared without response correction for the matrix effect.
the direct comparison of signal intensities between different biofluids, or between different analytes, in untargetd metabolomics is inaccurate and should not be used for data interpretation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the signal intensities between different analytes cannot be directly compared in untargeted non-quantitative experiments, and the signal intensities in different biological matrices cannot be directly compared without accounting for matrix effects.

the direct comparison of signal intensities between different biofluids or between different analytes is not accurate in non-quantitive metabolomics and that proper response corrections must be made in order to obtain reliable results.

the signal intensity of a single analyte in untargeted non-quantitative experiments cannot be directly compared between different biofluids or to other analytes in the untargeted data matrix without proper response corrections.
